items.title: Sage Burress
items.summary: A photographic home for a creative practice that spans modeling, content, and artistry.
items.body:
Sage Burress works across modeling, content creation, makeup, henna, travel promotions, and face painting. Her website brings that range into one place, with a portfolio and individual pages for each service.

The opening pairs a personal introduction with photography. A dedicated portfolio gives the images room, while the service navigation helps visitors find the kind of collaboration they have in mind.

A clear contact link gives visitors a route from discovering the work to getting in touch. It is a personal presence with enough structure to support several kinds of creative work.

items.title: Masonry Color Corrections
items.summary: Making a specialist service understandable through the masonry work itself.
items.body:
Masonry Color Corrections works on the color of installed brick, mortar, repairs, and additions. Its website explains a service whose value is often clearest when two surfaces are seen together.

Before-and-after photography and an interactive comparison put that difference at the center of the page. Service descriptions explain the kinds of matching and staining available, and the gallery gives visitors more examples to explore.

The estimate path asks for the project location, a description, and useful photographs. That gives a visitor a concrete next step after understanding the work.

items.title: Before a website rebuild, gather the right things.
items.summary: A practical starting point for a clearer brief: the audience, the work, the proof, and the next step.
items.body:
Start with what has changed. Perhaps the business offers a different service now, the work has become more focused, or the site no longer sounds like the people behind it. Write that change in a few sentences before collecting visual references. It gives the project a reason to exist.

Describe the person the site needs to help. What are they trying to understand? What might make them hesitate? What should they be able to decide after a visit? A specific visitor and a specific decision give the pages a useful job.

Gather evidence you can actually use. Choose photographs of real work, clear service descriptions, and project examples you have permission to publish. Keep the context with each example: what the visitor is looking at and why it matters. Leave out results you cannot support and client comments you do not have permission to share.

Choose a next step that fits the work. A portfolio might lead to a conversation about a collaboration. A specialist service may need a location, a description, and photographs before an estimate is possible. Ask for enough information to make the first exchange useful without making the visitor do the whole project brief at once.

Bring a short list of references, with reasons. A reference is more useful when you can say what you notice: the pace, the writing, the way images are presented, or how easily you found something. The aim is to explain a direction, not to assemble someone else's website.

Finish with the practical boundaries. Note the timing, budget range, people involved in decisions, and any content or account access still missing. A brief can contain open questions. Naming them makes it easier to decide what needs attention first.

You do not need polished copy to start. A rough account of the business, a few strong examples, and an honest description of what needs to change are enough for a useful first brief.
